CAPA: one capabilities file for many coding agents

CAPA is an open-source CLI that treats a project-root capabilities.yaml (or .json) as the source of truth for agent capabilities, then installs that declaration into coding-agent clients and, in managed and wrap modes, runs a local MCP gateway.

OfficeKit explainer 7 September 2026

Publisher: Infragate (github.com/infragate, infragate.ai). The README tagline is “The package manager and MCP gateway for AI coding agents.” That wording is the one to use; the package.json description omits the gateway.

Hard product rule: if a skill, server, rule, hook, or plugin is not in the capabilities file, CAPA will not manage it. Leftover files under .cursor/ or .claude/ are ignored unless they are declared (or written by passthrough or bootstrap).

CAPA is a local developer tool: a package manager plus an optional proxy on your machine. It is not an enterprise hosted MCP gateway. This document does not compare it to other gateway products.

Who this is for

Scope

For teams tired of copying skills and MCP configs across Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Windsurf, and others; and for people who want a version-controlled agent setup they can clone with the repo.

Not a full schema or CLI handbook, an org-specific adoption pitch, or a promise of feature parity across every named agent. Getting started below is a short evaluator loop, not a tutorial from scratch.

The problem CAPA claims to solve

This section restates CAPA’s own product framing (the README “Why CAPA?” copy, restated more softly on capa.sh). It is not independent research about what all teams experience.

CAPA’s story is that agent config is scattered: CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules/, AGENTS.md, MCP JSON, hooks, and skill folders. Teammates diverge; nothing is pinned; cloning the repository does not clone the agent setup.

The proposed collapse is one version-controlled capabilities file plus a local MCP gateway that the CLI can start for you.

Read that as the problem CAPA claims to solve, not as a survey finding about how teams actually work.

One file, many clients, optional local proxy

In managed and wrap modes, coding agents talk MCP to a CAPA process on your machine. That process proxies to whatever upstream MCP you declared (stdio, HTTP, or SSE). The gateway also exposes on-demand meta-tools (setup_tools / call_tool), filtered endpoints per sub-agent, and an activity tracer that feeds a local project UI on the same origin as the server.

The default hub is around http://localhost:5912. Nothing here is a hosted control plane.

What goes in capabilities.yaml

The capabilities file is the declaration CAPA will honor. Official docs show this skeleton (from the capa.sh Capabilities file page): 

providers:
  - cursor
  - claude-code
options:
  toolExposure: expose-all  # expose-all | on-demand | none
skills: []
servers: []
tools: []
# rules, plugins, hooks, subagents, agents

JSON is accepted as well as YAML. If providers is omitted, CAPA can take -p, a stored preference, or a TTY prompt.

Roles of the main capabilities-file sections (one sentence each).
Section Role
providers Which coding-agent clients to install for.
options toolExposure; optional security; optional requiresCommands.
skills Instructional SKILL.md trees (inline, remote, GitHub/GitLab, local, installed, or plugin).
servers MCP backends: local cmd/args/env or remote url/headers.
tools MCP bindings (@server plus an upstream tool name) or shell command tools.
rules Durable guidance; Cursor .mdc files or folded instruction markers.
plugins GitHub/GitLab packages unpacked into skills, servers, tools, rules, hooks, and sub-agents.
hooks Lifecycle hooks, tagged capa:<id> in provider configs.
agents Base plus additional snippets for instruction files.
subagents Named specialists with skill and tool allow-lists.

Secrets use ${VarName} placeholders. They are not shell environment expansion into hooks by default.

After edits, run capa install. User docs say to restart the server (capa restart) only if server commands, env, or toolExposure changed; skill, rule, hook, and agents content apply on the next install. That restart rule is documented on the capabilities-file page and was not independently re-checked against the binary for this explainer.

Three ways to apply CAPA

Managed, wrap, and passthrough are distinct. “Passthrough” itself is two related paths — capa add --passthrough versus capa install --passthrough — and they should not be collapsed into one story.

How the three modes differ on command, config location, and proxy.
Mode Command Config location Local CAPA server / MCP proxy
Managed capa install Written into the real project Yes; install starts the server
Wrap capa wrap <provider> Shadow workspace under ~/.capa/workspaces Yes; wrap uses CAPA’s layout
Passthrough capa add --passthrough / capa install --passthrough Native provider files in the project No proxy management

README: capa add --passthrough skips the capabilities file, lockfile, and managed-file tracking; tool aliases still need managed mode. User docs: capa install --passthrough still reads the capabilities file but skips the gateway.

Tool exposure and why on-demand exists

options.toolExposure controls what the agent sees on tools/list and whether CAPA writes project MCP config files. capa.sh documents the mechanism without treating it as a universal cost saving.

toolExposure values and their effect on tools/list and project MCP files.
options.toolExposure tools/list Project MCP config files
expose-all (default) Full schemas for tools required by active skills Written
on-demand Only setup_tools and call_tool Written
none Empty Not written / previously written entries removed; capa sh still works

Sub-agents get a filtered MCP endpoint at /{projectId}/agents/{id}/mcp. Cursor keeps a single main capa MCP entry; Claude Code registers capa-{id}. Under toolExposure: none, instruction files may still be written, but project MCP entries are not.

Agent coverage

Marketing floors disagree: GitHub’s description says “30+” agents; capa.sh llms.txt says “35+”. Neither is a precise headcount. User docs list 39 named providers (20 “Full MCP integration” plus 19 “Skills-only”) as of the research access date. Skills-only providers do not get a project-local CAPA MCP server entry. “Dozens of named providers” is safer than treating any of those floors as a census.

Five providers named in the brief, with capa.sh MCP tier and wrap support.
Provider ID User-docs MCP tier Wrappable?
Cursor cursor (agent = CLI) Full MCP Yes (GUI + CLI alias)
Claude Code claude-code (claude) Full MCP Yes
Codex codex Full MCP Yes
GitHub Copilot github-copilot Full MCP No (shared .github/ / .vscode/)
Windsurf windsurf Skills-only (no project MCP registration on capa.sh) No

Windsurf taxonomy variance: a maintainer matrix marks Windsurf bold/full for rules, while capa.sh Providers is skills-only for MCP. This document follows capa.sh for user-facing copy.

Wrappable today (do not invent more): cursor, agent, claude-code/claude, codex, gemini-cli, opencode, qwen-code, kiro-cli, iflow-cli, kimi-cli.

Hooks are not universal. Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini CLI are wired; others warn and skip.

Illustrative native layouts: Cursor uses .cursor/rules/, .cursor/mcp.json, .cursor/skills/; Claude Code uses .claude/agents/, .mcp.json, CLAUDE.md; Copilot uses .vscode/mcp.json and .github/copilot-instructions.md.

Skills, plugins, and registries

Skills can be inline, remote, GitHub, GitLab, local, installed, or plugin. requires binds tools. Under on-demand exposure, skills without requires get no tools.

Plugins are not opaque blobs. CAPA clones the package and parses Claude (.claude-plugin/) or Cursor (.cursor-plugin/) manifests. Other formats (Augment, Droid, Kode) are not parsed today, according to maintainer docs.

Registries use types github, gitlab, url, and claude-marketplace. Adapters land in ~/.capa/registries-managed/. The README flags that most adapters are executable TypeScript — review before enabling third-party registries. Seeded catalogs mentioned in official copy include skills.sh, Cursor Marketplace, and Claude plugins.

After capa init, a bundled /bootstrap skill can scan a repo and draft config. That behavior is documented in the README and present in the repo tree; it was not exercised in the research pass behind this document.

Local hub: CLI, lockfile, and Web UI

The managed loop is capa init → capa add … → capa install → capa status / capa sh.

Install from official docs (do not add unverified flags). Latest stable CLI at research access (2026-09-07) is v2.1.2 (published 2026-08-26). That is the GitHub Releases tag, not the package.json "version": "1.0.0" string.

Manual binaries are on GitHub Releases.

capabilities.lock pins remote git refs; docs say commit it. Cache commands are capa cache and capa cache clean.

The Web UI is on the same origin as the local server: credentials, a capabilities editor, registries, OAuth, and activity traces. Wrap workspace paths are refused as projects.

Credentials live in a local CAPA database under ~/.capa/. Official pages disagree on the filename, so this document does not assert one. Official credentials docs do not describe a storage-encryption guarantee.

Getting started

Enough for an evaluator to try CAPA. For flags and edge cases, use the official Quick Start pages rather than inventing combinations.

  1. Install the CLI with the macOS/Linux or Windows command in the previous section.
  2. Run capa init in a project.
  3. Optionally use the bundled bootstrap skill (documented in the README) to draft a first capabilities file from an existing repo.
  4. Add a provider, skill, or server with capa add. See Quick Start (managed) for the documented sequence.
  5. Apply with capa install (managed), or capa wrap <provider> if you do not want CAPA to write into the real tree. Wrap walkthrough: Quick Start (wrap).
  6. Open the local UI (same origin as the server, default around port 5912) and restart the agent as the docs for that provider require.

What this document does not claim

Several numbers and badges appear in CAPA marketing copy. They are easy to over-read. This box is the rule for this explainer.

Topics this document will not treat as established product facts.
Topic How this document treats it
GitHub stars / forks Omitted. Snapshot counts change daily and are not a product boast here.
Agent counts Use “dozens of named providers (39 on capa.sh as of research)” or note that “30+” / “35+” marketing floors disagree. Not a precise headcount.
Token savings Mechanism of on-demand tools is documented; a README percentage claim is omitted here (unaudited vendor figure, not a general saving).
License Public GitHub repository. An SPDX license file was not confirmed in research (README badge says MIT; GitHub license was null and LICENSE 404’d). “Open source” here means the public repo, not a confirmed OSI license.
Security policy SECURITY.md lists security@infragate.co as a contact. Do not treat its supported-version table as current against v2.1.2.
Competitive positioning Unverified. Omitted.
